latin.375: §. IV. Errori primo successit SECUNDUS, perversa scil. intelligentia ac interpretatio Patrum Mediorum Seculorum, post Chalcedonense scil. seu postremum Concilium Oecumenicum, Eutychi oppositum, istius hæresin verò impugnantium argumento inter alia eô quoque, quô humanam Christi naturam ne exaltatam quidem, post Unionem cum divina personalem, à Divina magis absorberi statuerunt, quàm panis absorbetur à corpore Christi, in legitimo Eucharistiæ usu, isti uniendo.
latin.376: Loca hujusmodi aliquot, eademque omnino, in medium adducunt Reverendissimus Burnetus in Expositione 39. articulorum Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ pag. 330. & doctissimus Picherellus Opuscula Theol. p. 176, Chrysostomi scil. ad Cæsareum Monachum scribentis: Sicut antequam sanctificatur panis, panem nominamus: Divina autem illum sanctificante gratiâ, mediante sacerdote, liberatus est quidem ab appellatione panis, dignus autem habitus est Dominici corporis appellatione, & signatura panis in ipso permanfit. THEODORETI in Dialogo ita loquentis: Neque signa mystica post sanctificationem recedunt à sua natura: Manent enim in priore substantia & figura & forma & videri & tangi possunt, suntque panis &c. intelliguntur autem ea quæ sunt & creduntur, Dialogo secundo.
latin.377: GELASII denique contra Eutychen ita disputantis: Sacramenta, inquit, quæ sumimus, divina res est, & tamen non desinit esse substantia & natura panis & vini. His adjicimus PROSPERUM, Scriptorem per omnia Catholicum, disertè docentem: Eucharistiam duabus constare visibili elementorum specie & invisibili Dn. nostri sanguine & carne (hoc est Sacramento & re sacramenti) sicut persona Christi constat ex Deo & homine, Distinct. secunda de consecratione cap. Hoc est.
latin.378: Quæ loca omnia, in id Primariò intenta, ne crederetur, post spiritualem corporis Christi, cum pane, in Eucharistia, ritè debitèque celebrata, Unionem, panis abolitionem quandam seu absorbitionem contingere, istuc flectere sustinuerunt quotquot ad Consubstantiationem sibi aditum pararunt, ut post consecrationem panis, cum hoc ipso, etiam ante usum ejus, Corpus Christi non alio modo uniri sibi imaginarentur, quàm, post benedictam inter mulieres ab Angelo salutatam matrem Christi, in hujus utero, conceptæ humanæ Christi naturæ divina persona, substantiali sese modo, sociavit cumque ista in unum idemque ὑφιστάμενον unita est.
latin.379: Accessit tandem TERTIUS error, Seculo nono & undecimo subnatus, ex partim crudè intellectis Bertrami, alias Ratramni, in libro de corpore Christi ad Carol. Calvum, de figura corporis Christi in S. Coena, ad mentem antiquiorum Patrum, enunciatis, alibi recitandis integris; partim crudè nimis, de eadem figura corporis Christi, Berengarii effatis, utut non ita crudè ab ipso acceptis, debitus: His enim sese opponentium plurimi, ita panem corporis Christi figuram negarunt in Eucharistia sacra esse, ut Corporalem hujus cum isto Unionem urserint, sicque conceptum fotumque hactenus Consubstantiationis embryonem, vel crassiorem, vel subtiliorem, in lucem publicam prodire fecerint.

pass_a.375: §. IV. To the first error succeeded a SECOND — namely a perverse understanding and interpretation of the Fathers of the Middle Ages after Chalcedon, that is the last Ecumenical Council opposed to Eutyches, who in fighting his heresy used among other arguments also this: that Christ’s human nature, even exalted, after personal Union with the divine, is not absorbed by the Divine more than bread is absorbed by Christ’s body in the legitimate use of the Eucharist, when united to it.
pass_a.376: Several such places, and altogether the same ones, the Most Reverend Burnet brings into the middle in his Exposition of the 39 Articles of the Anglican Church p. 330, and the most learned Picherellus Opuscula Theologica p. 176 — namely Chrysostom writing to the monk Caesarius: Just as before the bread is sanctified we name it bread: but when divine grace sanctifies it, the priest mediating, it is freed indeed from the appellation of bread, yet is counted worthy of the appellation of the Lord’s body, and the signature of bread remained in it. And Theodoret speaking thus in the Dialogue: Nor do the mystical signs after sanctification withdraw from their nature: For they remain in the prior substance and figure and form and can be seen and touched, and are bread &c.; but they are understood as what they are and are believed, in the second Dialogue.
pass_a.377: Finally Gelasius disputing thus against Eutyches: The Sacraments, he says, which we take are a divine thing, and yet do not cease to be the substance and nature of bread and wine. To these we add Prosper, a Writer Catholic in all things, expressly teaching: that the Eucharist consists of two — the visible species of the elements and the invisible blood and flesh of our Lord (that is, the Sacrament and the thing of the sacrament) just as Christ’s person consists of God and man — Distinction 2 on consecration, chapter This is.
pass_a.378: All which places, primarily aimed lest it be believed that after the spiritual Union of Christ’s body with the bread in the Eucharist duly and rightly celebrated some abolition or absorption of the bread occurs — all who prepared themselves an entrance to Consubstantiation have borne to bend them thither, so that after consecration of the bread they imagined Christ’s Body united to it even before its use in no other way than that, after the mother of Christ blessed among women and greeted by the Angel, the divine person associated itself in a substantial mode with the human nature of Christ conceived in her womb and was united with it into one and the same ὑφιστάμενον.
pass_a.379: There came at length a THIRD error, born under the ninth and eleventh centuries, owed partly to crudely understood utterances of Bertram, otherwise Ratramnus, in the book On the body of Christ to Charles the Bald, on the figure of Christ’s body in the Sacred Supper after the mind of the older Fathers — to be recited entire elsewhere — partly to Berengar’s sayings on the same figure of Christ’s body, taken too crudely, even if not so crudely by him: for very many of those opposing them so denied that the bread is a figure of Christ’s body in the sacred Eucharist that they urged a Corporal Union of this with that, and so made the Consubstantiation embryo hitherto conceived and fostered — whether crasser or subtler — come forth into public light.

375: §.IV: after the first error comes a SECOND — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon, read askew.
Fighting Eutyches they said Christ’s exalted human nature is not absorbed by the divine more than bread is absorbed by Christ’s body in legitimate Eucharistic use.
376: Burnet (39 Articles p. 330) and Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 176) stack the same loci.
Chrysostom to Caesarius: after sanctification the bread is worthy of the Lord’s-body name, yet the bread-signature remains.
Theodoret’s Dialogue II: the mystical signs keep prior substance, figure, and form — still bread to sight and touch, understood as believed.
377: Gelasius against Eutyches: what we take is a divine thing, yet does not cease to be the substance and nature of bread and wine.
Prosper: Eucharist = visible element-species + invisible Lord’s flesh and blood (sacrament and res), as Christ’s person is God and man.
378: Those texts first meant to block belief that after spiritual bread–body union the bread is abolished or absorbed.
Consubstantiation-seekers bend them instead: after consecration, even before use, they imagine union like the divine person joining Christ’s human nature in Mary’s womb into one ὑφιστάμενον.
379: THIRD error (9th–11th c.): crudely heard Bertram/Ratramnus on the figure of Christ’s body (to Charles the Bald), plus Berengar’s figure-sayings taken too raw.
Opponents denied figure so hard they urged corporal union — and so forced the long-fostered Consubstantiation embryo, crass or subtle, into public light.
Stop before §.V (Paschasius Radbertus as alleged first author).

notes.378: Anti-absorption bent to ante-usum hypostatic analogy.
